prompt: A quantitative equity team receives a fundamental dataset in which young firms often lack long operating histories and some distressed firms stop reporting selected fields. The PM proposes deleting every row containing a missing value because "the remaining data will be clean. " The research lead asks how that choice could affect a model intended to score the full investable universe.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Deleting all incomplete rows can bias the sample if missingness is related to firm characteristics.
statements.explanation: Systematic missingness can cause deletion to change the population represented by the sample.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Complete-case deletion is harmless whenever the resulting dataset remains large.
statements.explanation: A large retained sample can still be systematically unrepresentative.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A flag indicating that a value was missing may contain predictive information.
statements.explanation: The reporting failure itself may be associated with age, distress, or another relevant condition.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Any imputed number should be treated as though it were an observed measurement with no uncertainty.
statements.explanation: Imputation is an estimate and can alter uncertainty and relationships in the data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The team should compare the characteristics of retained and removed firms before adopting the deletion rule.
statements.explanation: This comparison can reveal whether the rule disproportionately excludes certain types of firms.

prompt: A risk team is modeling bond spreads using several financial ratios. Missing leverage values are replaced with the median calculated from the entire ten-year dataset before the observations are divided into training and test periods. An analyst argues that median imputation is always safe because it does not use the target variable. The team asks you to identify the flawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The following claim is false: Median imputation can be more resistant to extreme observed values than mean imputation.
statements.explanation: The median is less affected by extreme values than the mean.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Computing the median from the entire dataset allows information from the test period to influence preprocessing.
statements.explanation: The preprocessing parameter reflects observations that are supposed to remain held out.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The absence of direct target values in the calculation guarantees that the evaluation remains uncontaminated.
statements.explanation: Test-feature information can still influence model development and make the evaluation less independent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The imputation value should normally be estimated using the training data and then applied to the test data.
statements.explanation: Fitting preprocessing only on training data preserves the intended separation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Replacing all missing values with one median can reduce the apparent variability of that feature.
statements.explanation: Repeated use of a central value creates an artificial concentration in the feature distribution.

prompt: A trading desk combines prices from multiple vendors. A missing quote can mean either a temporary feed outage or that an illiquid security did not trade, and the head trader wants every gap forward-filled so the model always receives a complete matrix. The team must decide whether one rule is appropriate for both causes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Forward-filling assumes that the last observed value is a reasonable substitute until a new observation arrives.
statements.explanation: Forward-filling explicitly carries the previous observation into later missing positions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A feed outage and a no-trade interval necessarily carry the same economic information.
statements.explanation: One is a data-system failure, while the other may reflect market liquidity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Long forward-filled stretches can make stale prices appear current.
statements.explanation: Repeated old values can conceal the fact that no current price was observed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Recording the duration or reason for missingness may help distinguish stale data from genuine observations.
statements.explanation: Missingness metadata can preserve information that a filled value alone would discard.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Once missing values are filled, the team no longer needs to examine how the missingness arose.
statements.explanation: The missingness mechanism affects whether an imputation rule is defensible and how the result should be interpreted.

prompt: You are a Quantitative Researcher analyzing a dataset of historical corporate bond prices to build a predictive model for credit spread movements. You discover that for several small-cap issuers, the "Daily Trading Volume" field is frequently missing. Upon further investigation, you realize these gaps occur primarily during periods of extreme market volatility when liquidity for these specific bonds evaporates entirely.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In this context, the missing data is "Missing at Random" (MAR), as the missingness is related to the observed volatility in the broader market rather than the unobserved trading behavior of the small-cap bonds themselves.
statements.explanation: If the data is missing because the volume was too low to record or the market didn't trade (which is the variable itself), it is Missing Not at Random (MNAR).

statements.label: B
statements.text: Replacing the missing volume data with the mean volume of the entire dataset (mean imputation) would likely lead to an underestimation of the model's risk, as it ignores the informative nature of the missingness.
statements.explanation: Mean imputation artificially reduces variance and fails to capture the "signal" that the missing data represents a state of zero liquidity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dropping all rows with missing volume data (complete case analysis) is the most robust strategy here, as it ensures the model is trained only on high-quality, verified data points without introducing imputation noise.
statements.explanation: Dropping rows (Listwise deletion) during volatile periods would lead to "survivorship bias" in the training set, as the model would never learn how the market behaves during the most critical stress events. (Ref: Handbook of AI Ch. 2.4)

statements.label: D
statements.text: The fact that data is missing specifically during liquidity crunches suggests that the "missingness" itself is a highly informative feature that could serve as a proxy for market stress.
statements.explanation: In trading, a "null" result in a liquidity field is often a signal that the asset is untradeable, which is vital information for a risk model.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the missingness is "Missing Not at Random" (MNAR), any imputation strategy that does not explicitly model the cause of the missing data will likely introduce significant systematic bias into the strategy's backtest.
statements.explanation: When the reason for missingness is tied to the values themselves, standard statistical fixes often distort the true relationship between features and targets.

prompt: You are a Quantitative Strategist developing a model to trade "Distressed Debt. " Your primary feature is the "Interest Coverage Ratio" (Earnings / Interest Expense). In your dataset of 5,000 firms, you find that 15% of the values are missing. Further analysis reveals that 10% of these missing values belong to firms that have recently defaulted and ceased filing financial statements, while the other 5% are missing due to a technical error in the data provider's API. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 5% of data missing due to the API error is "Missing Completely at Random" (MCAR), and dropping these specific rows would likely not introduce systematic bias into the model.
statements.explanation: Since an API glitch is unrelated to the firms' actual performance, it is MCAR; deleting these rows reduces sample size but doesn't skew the results.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 10% of data missing from defaulted firms is "Missing Not at Random" (MNAR), as the reason for the missingness is directly related to the poor financial health of the companies.
statements.explanation: The missingness is a "Selection Effect" caused by the bankruptcy process itself.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dropping all missing values (Listwise Deletion) is the safest approach because it avoids the "hallucination" of financial ratios for companies that no longer exist.
statements.explanation: Deleting the defaulted firms creates "Survivorship Bias. " The model would only learn what successful distressed debt looks like, leading to a massive overestimation of the strategy's expected returns.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If you choose to impute the missing ratios for the defaulted firms using the "Sector Average, " the model will likely develop an optimistic bias, as it replaces "failing" metrics with "average" ones.
statements.explanation: Imputing the average for a company that has zero earnings and high debt hides the "signal" of failure, making the model blind to the primary risk it's supposed to manage.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A more rigorous "Data Discipline" approach would be to impute the API-error gaps while treating the defaulted-firm gaps as a distinct category or assigned "floor" value to reflect their distressed state.
statements.explanation: Professional quant workflows often use different strategies for different "types" of missingness within the same column.

prompt: You are a Quantitative Researcher backtesting a strategy that utilizes "Intraday Sentiment Scores" derived from news headlines. You notice that the sentiment data is missing for several hours each day during the Asian trading session. You are considering two different strategies to handle this missingness: 1. Zero Imputation: Filling the gaps with a score of 0 (neutral). 2. Mean Imputation: Filling the gaps with the average sentiment score of the entire 5-year training dataset. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Zero imputation in this context is likely to introduce a "conservative bias, " as it forces the model to assume a neutral market state during periods where sentiment might actually be trending.
statements.explanation: Arbitrarily setting values to zero (neutral) dampens the signal and makes the model less reactive to potential overnight shifts. (

statements.label: B
statements.text: Mean imputation is a superior strategy because it ensures the model remains "centered" on the long-term average sentiment, preventing erratic trades during the Asian session.
statements.explanation: Mean imputation blunts the signal and ignores the specific temporal context of the data, often leading to poor live performance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Mean imputation introduces "Look-Ahead Bias" because the global average is calculated using data from the future relative to the missing observations in the early years of the backtest.
statements.explanation: Using a "global mean" from a full dataset is a classic data discipline violation, as that mean incorporates information that was not yet known.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the news provider only fails to report sentiment during periods of extreme market crashes (MNAR), both imputation strategies will systematically understate the strategy's historical risk (Drawdown).
statements.explanation: By filling "crash" periods with neutral or average scores, the model never "learns" the association between missing data and extreme losses.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Dropping the hours with missing data (Listwise Deletion) would be the most biased approach, as it would likely remove the very periods of "overnight" price discovery that are critical for morning gap strategies.
statements.explanation: Deleting temporal gaps in financial time-series destroys the continuity of price action, leading to a fragmented and unrealistic backtest. G2: Noise and Outliers

prompt: A market-data pipeline records a stock price of $9,800 between observations near $98. The operations manager wants the row removed immediately, while the PM notes that genuine price jumps can also appear extreme. The research team must investigate before changing the training set.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Comparing the observation with source records and corporate-action data can help determine whether it is an error.
statements.explanation: External context can distinguish a bad record from a legitimate event.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Every statistically extreme observation should be deleted before model training.
statements.explanation: Extremeness does not by itself imply that an observation is erroneous.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the value is a decimal-placement error, retaining it can distort learned relationships.
statements.explanation: A large erroneous value can exert disproportionate influence on some learners and statistics.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the value reflects a genuine market event, removing it may eliminate behavior the live model must handle.
statements.explanation: Rare but valid events can be important to the deployment environment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An observation's distance from the sample mean alone establishes whether it is invalid.
statements.explanation: Validity requires contextual and data-quality evidence, not only a statistical threshold.

prompt: A portfolio analytics group compares a linear regression model with a tree-based model for estimating transaction costs. A few trades have exceptionally large costs, and a junior analyst claims those observations must affect both learners in exactly the same way because both receive the same rows. The group wants to understand model sensitivity before deciding how to treat the trades. The team asks you to identify the flawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Large residuals can have strong influence on a least-squares regression fit because their errors are squared.
statements.explanation: Squared-error fitting gives large residuals disproportionate weight.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tree is completely immune to noisy or extreme observations.
statements.explanation: Outliers can affect split selection, leaf predictions, and tree stability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Different model families can react differently to the same outliers.
statements.explanation: Their structures and fitting criteria produce different sensitivities.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Increasing a tree's minimum leaf size may reduce its ability to isolate a single unusual observation.
statements.explanation: Larger leaves prevent very small groups from being modeled independently.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Removing the high-cost trades is automatically correct if doing so improves training error.
statements.explanation: The team must determine whether the trades are errors or valid cases and evaluate performance beyond the training sample.

prompt: A volatility model performs well on ordinary days but badly during a handful of market shocks. The PM calls those shock days "noise" and proposes winsorizing every extreme return, while the risk officer says those are precisely the days that matter most. The intended use is portfolio risk control during both normal and stressed markets.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether the shock observations should be retained depends partly on the model's intended use.
statements.explanation: Data treatment should reflect the conditions the model is expected to handle.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Labeling rare observations as noise is justified solely because they occur infrequently.
statements.explanation: Rare observations may be valid and economically important.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Winsorization changes extreme values and can understate the severity of genuine tail events.
statements.explanation: Capping replaces observed tail magnitudes with less extreme values.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The team can evaluate performance separately in ordinary and stressed regimes to expose the tradeoff.
statements.explanation: Segment-level evaluation shows whether average performance conceals stress failures.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A cleaning procedure that improves average error necessarily improves the model's usefulness for risk control.
statements.explanation: Average improvement may come at the cost of worse behavior during the most consequential periods.

prompt: You are training a linear regression model to predict the "Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio" of technology stocks. Your dataset contains a few "Penny Stocks" where the earnings are nearly zero, resulting in extreme P/E ratios (e.g., over 5,000), while the sector average is 30. You observe that the resulting regression line is pulled sharply toward these extreme values, significantly increasing the error for the rest of the stocks in your universe.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The extreme P/E ratios are examples of "Outliers" that have high leverage, meaning they disproportionately influence the slope of the linear regression line.
statements.explanation: In OLS regression, points far from the mean of the predictor variables exert high leverage and can dominate the parameter estimation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In this case, the best strategy is to keep the outliers and use an L2 loss function (Mean Squared Error), as this will force the model to prioritize fitting these high-impact observations.
statements.explanation: L2 loss squares the errors, actually increasing the penalty for outliers and making the model even more sensitive to them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A more "Robust" learner, such as a Support Vector Regressor or a model using Huber Loss, would be less sensitive to these extreme P/E ratios than a standard Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) model.
statements.explanation: Robust statistical methods are specifically designed to limit the influence of outliers on the final model parameters.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the extreme P/E ratios are the result of accurate financial reporting (not data errors), they must be kept in the dataset to ensure the model captures the full reality of the technology sector.
statements.explanation: Even if data is "accurate, " keeping outliers that don't represent the broader population can lead to poor generalization and high variance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The decision to remove these outliers should be based on whether they represent the "True Process" you are trying to model or if they are "Noise" that obscures the generalizable relationship for typical stocks.
statements.explanation: Data discipline requires a subjective judgment on whether an outlier is a "valid extreme" or an "irrelevant anomaly" for the specific trading objective.

prompt: You are a Quantitative Research Lead reviewing a proposed data-cleaning pipeline for a high-frequency trend-following strategy. The analyst suggests that because extreme price spikes in liquid markets like the S&P 500 E-mini futures are rare and often represent "untradeable" liquidity gaps, they should be treated as systematic errors and handled aggressively to keep the model's coefficients stable.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In a linear model using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), the squaring of residuals is an effective mechanism for naturally "de-weighting" outliers, ensuring they have less influence on the final parameters than the majority of the data.
statements.explanation: OLS is actually the most sensitive to outliers; squaring the residuals gives extreme values disproportionate leverage over the model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If a price spike is a valid market event (e.g., a reaction to a surprise interest rate hike), removing it via Trimming is considered best practice because it helps the model generalize to the "typical" market regimes it will face 99% of the time.
statements.explanation: Removing real market events via trimming creates "Survivorship Bias" and leads to a model that is unprepared for real-world risk, effectively "snooping" for a cleaner history.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Support Vector Regressor (SVR) using an ϵ-insensitive loss function is highly sensitive to outliers because it attempts to fit a hyperplane that encompasses every single data point, regardless of its distance from the mean.
statements.explanation: SVR with ϵ-insensitive loss is actually robust; it ignores errors smaller than 𝜖 and uses a linear (not squared) penalty for larger errors, similar to a Huber loss or MAE.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A Decision Tree learner is highly sensitive to the exact magnitude of outliers because it uses the variance of the entire feature column to determine the optimal location for every split.
statements.explanation: Trees are robust to outliers; once a value is beyond a split threshold, its specific magnitude (whether it's 100 or 1,000,000) does not change the tree's structure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Outliers that represent genuine but extreme market realizations should generally be retained or managed through robust loss functions (like Huber Loss) rather than being deleted, as they contain critical information about the "Fat Tails" of the risk distribution.
statements.explanation: Data discipline in finance requires distinguishing between "Bad Noise" (errors) and "Valid Extremes. " Valid extremes should be capped or modeled robustly, not erased.

prompt: You are a Quantitative Consultant auditing a "Risk Parity" fund that uses a high-capacity Neural Network to estimate covariance matrices. The fund's primary researcher argues that because the model is trained on decades of data, there is no need to manually address outliers or "flash crashes, " as the model will eventually learn to treat them as statistical anomalies.

statements.label: A
statements.text: High-capacity learners like Deep Neural Networks are naturally immune to outliers because the large volume of training data provides enough "normal" observations to cancel out the effect of extreme noise.
statements.explanation: High-capacity models are actually more prone to fitting outliers; they have the flexibility to "memorize" the anomaly as a complex rule rather than ignoring it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the dataset contains a "Broken Ticker" (e.g., a stock that erroneously reflects a price of $0.01 for one day), the neural network may attempt to "explain" this outlier by adjusting its weights, leading to a distorted feature space for all other stocks.
statements.explanation: This is the "leverage" effect; the model distorts its internal representation to minimize the massive loss associated with a clear data error.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Using Batch Normalization within the neural network architecture is a guaranteed way to eliminate the influence of outliers, as it scales all inputs to a mean of zero and unit variance regardless of their initial magnitude.
statements.explanation: Batch Normalization is sensitive to outliers; a single extreme value in a batch can skew the mean and variance for the entire batch, potentially "polluting" the training of normal samples.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In a professional trading environment, an outlier that is proven to be a "Data Integrity Error" should be removed or corrected, whereas an "Extreme Market Realization" should be managed using robust optimization or clipping.
statements.explanation: This is the core of data discipline: distinguish between "Bad Data" (delete) and "Hard Truths" (keep/manage).

statements.label: E
statements.text: If you use a Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss to train the network, a single 20-sigma outlier will have less impact on the final model than 1,000 small, 0.1-sigma noisy observations.
statements.explanation: Because MSE squares each error, a single 20-sigma outlier contributes a loss of 400, while 1,000 separate 0.1- sigma errors contribute a combined loss of only 10. Therefore, the single extreme outlier has far greater impact on the model. G3: Sampling Bias and Representativeness

prompt: A researcher builds a stock-selection model using only companies that remain in the S&P 500 at the end of the study period. The PM wants to use the backtest as evidence that the strategy would have worked throughout the prior decade. A risk analyst questions what happened to firms that left the index.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Restricting the history to current constituents can create survivorship bias.
statements.explanation: The sample is conditioned on surviving in the index until the end of the study.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Excluding firms that failed, merged, or were removed may make historical performance look better than it was.
statements.explanation: Removed firms can include poor outcomes that a survivor-only sample omits.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A large number of current constituents eliminates the selection problem.
statements.explanation: Sample size does not correct a systematic inclusion rule.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A point-in-time constituent history would better represent the securities available at each past date.
statements.explanation: It reconstructs the investable membership known at each time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Survivorship bias affects only descriptive statistics and cannot affect a trained model.
statements.explanation: Biased training examples can change learned relationships and evaluated performance.

prompt: A brokerage trains a client-churn model using responses from a voluntary satisfaction survey. Highly engaged clients and very dissatisfied clients respond most often, while the model will be applied to every client. The product director assumes that thousands of responses make the sample representative. The team asks you to identify the flawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The following claim is false: Voluntary response patterns can create selection bias.
statements.explanation: Participation is related to client characteristics rather than being random.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A large sample can still misrepresent the full client population.
statements.explanation: More observations reduce random uncertainty but do not remove systematic sampling bias.

statements.label: C
statements.text: High predictive accuracy within the respondent sample proves equivalent accuracy for nonrespondents.
statements.explanation: Performance may change in groups underrepresented or absent from development data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Comparing respondent and nonrespondent characteristics can help diagnose representativeness.
statements.explanation: Such comparisons can reveal systematic differences in coverage.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reweighting may help only if the team has useful information about how the sampled and target populations differ.
statements.explanation: Effective weighting requires variables that describe relevant selection differences.

prompt: A credit fund trains a default model entirely on large U.S. public companies from a period of low interest rates, then plans to score small private companies during a tightening cycle. The investment committee asks whether a random held-out subset with strong results is enough to approve deployment. The modeling team agrees that the split was technically clean.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A clean random split can estimate performance on observations drawn from a similar source population.
statements.explanation: Holding out source-population rows tests transfer within that sampled setting.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It guarantees representative evaluation for small private companies in a different rate environment.
statements.explanation: The deployment population and environment may differ materially.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Differences in company size, disclosure, and macroeconomic conditions can limit generalization.
statements.explanation: These differences can change both feature distributions and outcome relationships.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Evaluation data resembling the intended deployment population would provide more relevant evidence.
statements.explanation: Representative evaluation better supports the proposed real-world use.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sampling bias is impossible if no test rows were used during training.
statements.explanation: Train/test separation and population representativeness are distinct concerns.

prompt: You are a Quantitative Strategist backtesting a "High-Yield Dividend" strategy. Your dataset is comprised of all US-listed stocks that paid a dividend in the 2010–2020 period. You discover that many of the highest-performing stocks in your training set were small-cap companies that were eventually acquired by larger firms at a significant premium. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Training only on companies that paid a dividend ensures the sample is representative of the broader market, as dividend policy is a reliable proxy for overall corporate health and stability.
statements.explanation: Selecting for dividends is a specific filter that excludes growth stocks and non-dividend payers, making the sample unrepresentative of the total equity market.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This approach suffers from Selection Bias because the sample is restricted by a characteristic (paying a dividend) that is likely correlated with the factors you are trying to predict, such as low volatility or value.
statements.explanation: Selection bias occurs when the criteria for inclusion in the study (dividend payment) skews the distribution of the features and outcomes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The inclusion of stocks that were eventually acquired introduces a form of Survivorship Bias if your database only includes the price history of companies that are still trading under their own ticker today.
statements.explanation: If the "acquired" winners are missing from the data because they no longer have an active ticker, the backtest ignores a primary source of the strategy's potential historical return.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the 2010–2020 period was characterized by declining interest rates, the model will likely generalize to a high- rate environment because dividend-paying stocks are inherently resistant to changes in the discount rate.
statements.explanation: Dividend stocks often act as "bond proxies"; a model trained during falling rates will likely fail to understand the risk of these stocks underperforming when rates rise. (

statements.label: E
statements.text: A dataset consisting of 10 years of every dividend-paying stock in the US is sufficiently large to guarantee that any findings regarding "alpha" are a result of true market signals rather than sampling artifacts.
statements.explanation: Volume and duration do not eliminate systematic bias. If the sample is restricted to a specific "slice" of the market, the model remains a prisoner of that slice's unique regime.

prompt: You are developing a machine learning model to predict the probability of corporate bankruptcy. Your training set is constructed by gathering the financial statements of 10,000 firms listed on the NYSE and NASDAQ as of December 2025, and you label them based on whether they filed for Chapter 11 at any point between 2015 and 2025. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This sampling method is an effective way to capture a representative history of the market because it includes a decade of data across two of the world's largest stock exchanges.
statements.explanation: A sample of "currently existing" firms is not a representative history; it is a "winner's history" that omits the failures required for a balanced classification task.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The dataset is susceptible to Survivorship Bias because the selection criteria (being listed as of 2025) naturally excludes the very firms that the model is trying to identify—those that went bankrupt and were delisted prior to 2025.
statements.explanation: This is a classic example of survivorship bias. By looking backward from the present, you only see those that survived the interval, skewing the model's understanding of risk.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the firms in the sample are all from the NYSE and NASDAQ, the model's findings can be generalized to characterize the bankruptcy risks of small, private startups without further adjustments.
statements.explanation: This is a failure of representativeness. Publicly traded "Blue Chip" or mid-cap firms have fundamentally different risk profiles and data-generating processes than private startups.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is a form of Selection Bias where the sampling mechanism is correlated with the target variable, resulting in a dataset that is systematically missing the most critical "negative" outcomes.
statements.explanation: The selection filter (survival to 2025) is directly tied to the outcome (not being bankrupt), ensuring the training set lacks the necessary diversity of the target class.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Increasing the number of features in this specific dataset (e.g., adding more technical indicators) will fix the underlying sampling error and allow the model to generalize accurately to the total population of firms.
statements.explanation: You cannot fix a biased sample by adding more features. If the "failed" firms are missing from the rows, adding more columns only helps the model overfit the "survivor" bias.

prompt: You are building a model to predict the probability of success for clinical trials in the pharmaceutical industry. Your training dataset consists of every trial that was successfully completed and published in a major medical journal between 2010 and 2025. You plan to use this model to help a venture capital firm decide which early-stage drug candidates to fund.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The dataset is likely a representative sample of all clinical trials because major medical journals are the primary repository for high-quality scientific evidence and trial outcomes.
statements.explanation: Relying on published journals introduces a heavy filter; the "universe" of all trials is much larger and more diverse than the "universe" of published successes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This approach suffers from Selection Bias (specifically "Publication Bias") because trials that failed to meet their primary endpoints or showed negative results are significantly less likely to be published, creating an overly optimistic training set.
statements.explanation: Selection bias occurs when the data you can see is systematically different from the data you cannot see due to a filtering mechanism (like editorial approval).

statements.label: C
statements.text: Using a sample of 15 years of published trials provides a sufficient volume of data to ensure that the model can generalize to the total population of all drug development efforts.
statements.explanation: Volume and time duration cannot fix a sample that is fundamentally skewed toward one type of outcome. (

statements.label: D
statements.text: The model will likely underestimate the "True Failure Rate" of drug development because the "negative" outcomes— the thousands of trials that were discontinued or never published—are entirely missing from the training distribution.
statements.explanation: By training on a "sanitized" version of history, the model loses the ability to calculate the base rate of failure for the asset class.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A model trained on this biased sample will likely provide the venture capital firm with a false sense of security, as it has never learned to identify the subtle signals that precede a trial's failure or abandonment.
statements.explanation: Generalization requires the training data to be a "miniature version" of the real world; if the training data is 90% success but the real world is 90% failure, the model will fail in production. G4: Temporal Structure and Ordering

prompt: A team predicts next-day returns using ten years of daily observations. To obtain similar class proportions in both subsets, an analyst randomly shuffles all days before splitting them into training and test data. The PM asks whether the resulting score reflects how the model would actually have been developed and deployed through time. The team asks you to identify the flawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A chronological split better preserves the sequence in which past data become available for future prediction.
statements.explanation: It trains on earlier information and evaluates on later observations.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Random shuffling can place later market regimes in training while earlier observations appear in the test set.
statements.explanation: Shuffling ignores the direction in which information arrives.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Random shuffling is always valid whenever individual rows have distinct dates.
statements.explanation: Dated rows can still have temporal dependence and a forecasting deployment order.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Financial observations near one another in time may be dependent rather than exchangeable.
statements.explanation: Market conditions and overlapping signals can create serial dependence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Preserving order can make evaluation harder while still making it more realistic.
statements.explanation: A realistic future period may differ from the training period and produce a lower but more meaningful estimate.

prompt: A monthly trading model is evaluated with cross-validation. An engineer proposes ordinary random folds, while the research director proposes a walk-forward design that repeatedly trains on earlier months and evaluates on later months. Several features and labels are based on overlapping return windows.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The following claim is false: Walk-forward evaluation respects the intended past-to-future prediction direction.
statements.explanation: Each evaluation period is predicted using only preceding training periods.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Random folds can mix observations from both sides of a test month into its training set.
statements.explanation: Ordinary random assignment does not preserve chronological availability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Overlapping windows can make nearby observations share information and appear more independent than they are.
statements.explanation: Shared underlying days can increase dependence between nominally separate examples.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Every walk-forward fold must use the same number of training observations to be valid.
statements.explanation: Expanding-window designs legitimately use a growing training history.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Temporal validation design should reflect when inputs and labels would actually have been available.
statements.explanation: Availability timing determines whether the simulated prediction could have been made in practice.

prompt: A fund trains a model each Friday to trade the following week. Its dataset assigns each Friday observation a label equal to the return through the next Friday, but the training set includes the most recent Friday even though that label would not yet be known at the retraining time. The backtest developer says the row is historical now, so its use is acceptable.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The relevant question is whether the label was available at the simulated Friday decision time.
statements.explanation: A valid backtest must reproduce historical information availability.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Including the unresolved forward return gives the simulated model information it could not have had then.
statements.explanation: The future return becomes known only after the simulated training event.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A value's presence in today's completed database proves it was available at every earlier model-training date.
statements.explanation: Modern databases often contain values that were unknown at earlier points in time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The training cutoff may need to exclude observations whose label windows have not finished.
statements.explanation: Only labels realized by the cutoff can legitimately support that training run.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Respecting row dates alone is sufficient even when labels mature after those dates.
statements.explanation: Label availability can lag the observation timestamp and must also be considered.

prompt: A researcher is developing a "Mean Reversion" strategy. To improve the signal-to-noise ratio, they decide to normalize their features (like RSI and Bollinger Bands) by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation calculated over the entire 20-year historical dataset before splitting the data into training and testing sets. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It is incorrect to conclude that this preprocessing step is mathematically sound because using the global mean and standard deviation provides the model with a "Stable Reference Point" that remains consistent across all market regimes.
statements.explanation: The embedded claim is inaccurate, so rejecting it is correct. While it provides a "stable" point, it is an illegal point. A trader in 2010 cannot know the mean volatility of 2024 to normalize their data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Normalizing on the full dataset is an effective way to prevent Temporal Autocorrelation, as it ensures that each daily observation is scaled relative to the long-term equilibrium of the market.
statements.explanation: Scaling does not address autocorrelation; it merely changes the units of the features while simultaneously leaking future information into the past.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the normalization parameters (μ,σ) are based on the entire population, this technique is considered the most robust way to ensure that the model generalizes to "unseen" future data.
statements.explanation: It actually ruins generalization; the model learns to expect a specific "global" scale that it will never be able to calculate in live trading, where the "future" mean is unknown.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This process does not introduce Look-Ahead Bias because the normalization only affects the "Scale" of the features and does not reveal the actual "Direction" of future price movements to the model.
statements.explanation: This is a classic form of look-ahead bias; if the global mean is high, the model "knows" that future prices/volatility will be high, even if it hasn't "seen" those dates yet.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The model's high performance in the backtest is likely an artifact of Data Leakage, as the training samples now contain information about the mean and variance of the "future" test set that would not have been available to a trader in real- time.
statements.explanation: To avoid this, normalization parameters must be calculated only on the training set (or via a rolling window) and then applied to the test set.

prompt: You are implementing a "Walk-Forward" validation scheme for a trend-following algorithm. In this setup, you use a sliding window: you train on the first 3 years of data, test on the 4th year, then shift the entire window forward by 1 year and repeat.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This "Walk-Forward" methodology is the most robust way to evaluate a trading strategy because it preserves the Temporal Order of the data, ensuring the model is never tested on information that occurred chronologically before the training set.
statements.explanation: Walk-forward testing is the "Gold Standard" in finance because it maintains the arrow of time and simulates how a model would actually be deployed in a live environment.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Shuffling the individual days within each 3-year training window is a recommended step to ensure the model focuses on broad patterns rather than specific dates, and this does not introduce leakage since the test year remains untouched.
statements.explanation: Even within the training set, shuffling is harmful. Many financial features (like Momentum or Moving Averages) rely on the sequence of data; shuffling destroys the autocorrelation signals the model is meant to capture.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This approach helps the researcher detect Regime Drift, as the model's performance is evaluated across different chronological "slices" of the market (e.g., a low-volatility period followed by a high-volatility period).
statements.explanation: Because the model is retrained and retested as it moves through time, you can see exactly when and why a strategy begins to fail as market conditions evolve.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The "Walk-Forward" method is essentially a form of Data Leakage because the model "sees" the same historical patterns multiple times as the training window slides forward through the 20-year dataset.
statements.explanation: This is not leakage. As long as the test set for any given fold always follows the training set chronologically, the "future" remains unknown to the model at each step.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A potential drawback of this method is that it requires significantly more data than a standard split, as the early folds have very small training sets compared to the later folds in an "Expanding Window" variation.
statements.explanation: This is a practical constraint; your initial "Walk-Forward" results may be less reliable because the model was trained on a much smaller sample than the final results.

prompt: You are building a regime-switching model to pivot between an S&P 500 equity strategy and a cash position. One of your primary features is the "Macroeconomic Unemployment Rate. " Your backtesting script pulls the official Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) monthly unemployment figures, aligning the value for a given month (e.g., January's 4.0% unemployment) directly with the market price action on the final trading day of that same month (January 31). For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This temporal alignment is standard practice because matching the macroeconomic state of a specific calendar month with that month's closing stock prices ensures the model learns the exact contemporaneous relationship between the economy and the market.
statements.explanation: Aligning data based on the calendar month rather than the public release date allows the model to trade on information that was invisible to market participants at that time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This pipeline introduces a severe Forward-Looking Bias because the unemployment rate for a given month is typically not finalized, compiled, and publicly released by the government until the first or second Friday of the following month.
statements.explanation: This is a fatal look-ahead bias. If your model "knows" January's unemployment figures on January 31, it is cheating; those numbers are not known until the BLS release in early February.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because macroeconomic data is highly persistent and slow-moving, a 1- or 2-week reporting lag is statistically irrelevant and will not alter the model's predictive accuracy or signal generation in a live environment.
statements.explanation: In systematic trading, even a short informational lag is catastrophic. A model trained on unlagged data will exploit the "future" knowledge to avoid market downturns perfectly in the backtest, then fail completely in production.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is a classic example of a Timestamp Mismatch error, where the "event date" (when the economic activity occurred) is mistakenly treated as the "availability date" (when a trader could actually execute an order based on that data).
statements.explanation: To ensure valid time-series validation, financial models must utilize "Point-in-Time" data matrices that index observations by the exact publication timestamp rather than the period covered.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Running a random shuffle on the final dataset will neutralize this reporting lag by distributing the 45-day informational advantage evenly across both the training and validation sets.
statements.explanation: Shuffling does not fix a fundamental violation of causality; it simply spreads the corrupted, look-ahead signal across the entire dataset, guaranteeing an overfit model. G5: Train/Test Separation Discipline

prompt: A research team splits observations into training and test sets, but then standardizes every feature using the mean and standard deviation calculated from the combined data. The analyst notes that the test labels were never used and claims the test score is therefore fully independent. The PM asks whether the preprocessing design matters.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Combined-data standardization lets the test-feature distribution influence the training pipeline.
statements.explanation: The fitted means and standard deviations summarize held-out observations.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Avoiding test labels is the only requirement for an uncontaminated test set.
statements.explanation: Test features can also affect learned preprocessing and development choices.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Scaling parameters should normally be estimated from training data and then applied unchanged to test data.
statements.explanation: This simulates how new observations would be transformed after deployment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Preprocessing is part of the model-development pipeline for purposes of train/test separation.
statements.explanation: Data-dependent preprocessing choices must be learned without the final test set.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The contamination becomes acceptable if the same formula is applied to every row.
statements.explanation: Uniform application does not undo the use of test information when estimating the parameters.

prompt: A desk compares 40 model and hyperparameter combinations directly on its designated test set, selects the highest- scoring one, and reports that same score as the final performance estimate. The head of research calls the process efficient because each candidate was trained without the test rows. The validation set was not used.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Selecting among models based on test performance makes the test set part of model development.
statements.explanation: Test results influenced which configuration was chosen.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reported maximum score can be optimistic because it includes chance variation across many comparisons.
statements.explanation: The winner may partly reflect noise specific to that test sample.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A validation set could be used for model selection while reserving the test set for final evaluation.
statements.explanation: This separates selection from the final generalization estimate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The test set remains fully unseen merely because its rows were not used to fit candidate parameters.
statements.explanation: Viewing and acting on test scores is a form of exposure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Retraining the chosen configuration on the training data erases the information gained from test-based selection.
statements.explanation: The configuration choice still encodes what the team learned from the test set.

prompt: A vendor supplies a preselected feature list after evaluating hundreds of candidates on the full historical dataset. Your team then makes a fresh train/test split and fits only the supplied features, claiming the test is clean because your own code never inspected those rows before splitting. The investment committee wants to know whether the upstream selection matters. The team asks you to identify the flawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Feature selection performed on the full dataset can transmit information from future test rows into the pipeline.
statements.explanation: The selected list reflects relationships observed in the entire history.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A later split automatically removes contamination introduced by earlier data-dependent decisions.
statements.explanation: The prior selection decision remains informed by the future test observations.

statements.label: C
statements.text: To preserve separation, feature selection should be repeated using only the training portion.
statements.explanation: Data-dependent selection belongs inside the training process.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Documentation of how the vendor created the feature list is relevant to evaluating the claimed independence.
statements.explanation: Provenance determines whether held-out information shaped the features.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Contamination can occur through development choices even when test rows are never passed directly to the final fitting function.
statements.explanation: Indirect influence through preprocessing or selection can compromise an evaluation.

prompt: An analyst is building a cross-sectional equity model to predict the next-day returns of 500 tech stocks. Before splitting the 10-year dataset into a 70% training set and a 30% testing set, they handle missing values in their accounting features (such as debt-to-equity ratios) by applying a global median imputation across the entire dataset to maximize sample integrity.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This preprocessing pipeline is structurally sound because using a global median preserves the overarching cross- sectional distribution of the sector, ensuring that both the train and test splits have identical feature spaces.
statements.explanation: Preserving the global distribution at the cost of leaking test-set data into the training phase destroys the validity of the out-of-sample evaluation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This approach introduces Data Contamination (Leakage) because the median values used to fill gaps in the training set are partially calculated using information from the future test set, violating the rule of absolute separation.
statements.explanation: This is a classic preprocessing leak. If test-set values influence the training set's features (even through a summary statistic like a median), the test data is no longer truly "unseen. "

statements.label: C
statements.text: Since median imputation only replaces missing values and does not alter the existing, non-missing data points, it cannot leak directional price signals or cause an artificial inflation of backtest performance.
statements.explanation: Even non-directional summary statistics leak information about the variance and scale of the future data space, which allows the model to adapt to the test distribution prematurely.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is a common violation of proper splitting where information from the out-of-sample period is inadvertently mixed into the in-sample training phase, leading to overly optimistic generalization metrics.
statements.explanation: This contamination masks how the model would actually handle missing data in real-time streaming environments where future medians are mathematically unavailable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: To maintain strict train/test discipline, the analyst must compute the median parameters using only the training data, and then apply those pre-calculated metrics to impute any missing values found in the test set.
statements.explanation: All feature engineering, scaling, and imputation parameters must be fit strictly on the training partition to ensure zero downstream contamination.

prompt: A researcher is building a model to predict the credit default risk of small businesses using a 10-year dataset. To address a high rate of missing values in the "Annual Revenue" column, they decide to use K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Imputation. They pass the entire feature matrix (the full 10 years of data) into the imputer to ensure the "neighbors" found for each missing value are as accurate as possible, then they perform a chronological 80/20 train-test split.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This methodology is an advanced form of data cleaning that improves model robustness by ensuring the training set's feature distributions are as complete and accurate as possible before the split.
statements.explanation: While accuracy is improved, it is "illegal" accuracy. You have contaminated the training phase with data points that, in a real-world scenario, would be in the "unknown future. "

statements.label: B
statements.text: This approach violates Train/Test Separation Discipline because the imputed values in the training set are calculated using the feature values of "neighbors" that reside in the future test set.
statements.explanation: This is a classic "Transductive Leak. " If a row from 2018 is missing data and its nearest neighbor is found in 2024, the 2018 row now contains information derived from the future.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Since KNN imputation only uses feature values (X) to fill gaps and does not look at the target labels (y), this process is considered "leakage-free" and safe for financial time-series applications.
statements.explanation: Leakage is not limited to labels. If the features in your training set are influenced by the features in your test set, the model will develop a "hidden familiarity" with the test distribution.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is an example of Manifold Contamination, where the underlying structure of the test set is "leaked" into the training set through the proximity calculations of the imputation algorithm.
statements.explanation: By using the entire dataset to define the "neighborhoods, " the researcher has allowed the geometry of the future to warp the representation of the past.

statements.label: E
statements.text: To maintain proper discipline, the researcher must fit the KNN imputer only on the training data, and then use that fitted model to impute missing values in both the training and test sets.
statements.explanation: Strict discipline requires that the "rules" for imputation are learned solely from the past. If the training set cannot stand alone to solve its own missing data, the split is compromised.

prompt: A quantitative developer is building a high-frequency market-making model. To optimize the model's performance, they perform Feature Selection (e.g., Recursive Feature Elimination) using the entire available 5-year dataset. After identifying the top 10 most predictive features, they then apply a Walk-Forward Validation scheme to train and test the model using only those 10 features.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This workflow is a statistically sound way to reduce the "Curse of Dimensionality, " ensuring the model only focuses on the most robust signals before entering the validation phase.
statements.explanation: Reducing dimensionality is good, but doing it by peeking at the test set creates a "survivor" set of features that are tailored to a future they shouldn't know yet.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This approach constitutes a Global Information Leak, as the decision of which features to include was informed by looking at the price action and volatility of the entire out-of-sample period.
statements.explanation: This is a common and subtle violation. If you use the test set to decide how to build your model (including which variables to use), the test set is no longer an independent measure of performance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the actual "Training" of the model weights happens within a walk-forward split, the initial feature selection process is considered an "Independent Preprocessing Step" and does not contaminate the test results.
statements.explanation: Feature selection is part of the model-building process. If the selection "sees" the future, the resulting "independent" training is already biased toward those future-relevant features.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is an example of Selection Bias (also known as "Data Snooping"), where the features chosen are likely those that happened to perform well over the specific 5-year window by chance, leading to a massive overestimation of live performance.
statements.explanation: This "snooping" results in features that look like "Universal Truths" in the backtest but are actually just artifacts of that specific historical period.

statements.label: E
statements.text: To maintain proper train/test separation, feature selection must be performed dynamically within each training fold of the walk-forward split, using only the data available up to that point in time.
statements.explanation: In a real-world scenario, a trader must decide which indicators to use without knowing which ones will be most profitable next year. Your validation must mimic this ignorance. G6: Data Snooping and Reuse

prompt: A quant team evaluates a strategy on the same 2018–2025 test period every week. After each disappointing result, it changes features, holding periods, or learners until the backtest looks strong. The team never explicitly copies test labels into the training matrix, so the PM believes the final test result remains unbiased. The team asks you to identify the flawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Repeatedly modifying the strategy in response to the same test results makes that period part of development.
statements.explanation: Feedback from the test period guides the evolving design.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The final performance estimate may capture chance patterns peculiar to the reused period.
statements.explanation: Enough iterations can adapt the strategy to sample-specific noise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Leakage is impossible unless test labels appear as training features.
statements.explanation: Information can leak through human selection and iteration without direct feature copying.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A genuinely untouched evaluation period would provide stronger evidence about the final design.
statements.explanation: It tests the selected design on observations that did not shape it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Keeping a written record of experiments can reveal the extent of repeated search, although it does not by itself restore test independence.
statements.explanation: Experiment tracking improves transparency but cannot make previously used data unseen again.

prompt: A fund screens 5,000 technical indicators on one historical period and publishes the ten with the best Sharpe ratios. It then presents those same ten in-sample results as evidence that the signals are economically meaningful. The CIO asks whether multiple comparisons change how the winners should be interpreted.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Searching many weak or useless indicators can still produce apparently strong winners by chance.
statements.explanation: Extreme results can arise from random variation when enough candidates are tried.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Selecting the maximum observed Sharpe ratio tends to favor positive estimation noise.
statements.explanation: Selection favors estimates that benefited from unusually favorable sample noise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The ten winners are validated because they outperformed the other 4,990 indicators on the search data.
statements.explanation: Ranking within the search sample is not independent confirmation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Testing the chosen indicators on untouched data can help distinguish persistent signal from selection luck.
statements.explanation: Fresh evidence avoids reusing the sample that produced the winners.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The number of alternatives examined is irrelevant once only the winners are reported.
statements.explanation: The breadth of the search affects how surprising the winning values really are.

prompt: Three research teams independently use the same corporate "golden" holdout period for final evaluation. They share their scores at monthly meetings, abandon weak ideas, and develop replacements based on what succeeded for the other teams. Governance records still label the period "untouched" because no one retrains directly on its rows.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The following claim is false: Organization-wide feedback can cause the holdout to influence later model designs.
statements.explanation: Shared results shape which approaches the organization pursues.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A holdout remains independent indefinitely as long as its raw rows are access-controlled.
statements.explanation: Repeated outcome feedback can compromise independence without exposing raw rows.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Aggregate scores can reveal enough information to guide adaptation to the holdout.
statements.explanation: Teams learn which choices worked on that specific period and respond accordingly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Limiting evaluation frequency and reserving a newer final set can reduce the risk of institutional overfitting.
statements.explanation: Reduced exposure and fresh final data preserve a more credible evaluation boundary.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Models selected through this process may have performance estimates that are too optimistic for genuinely new data.
statements.explanation: The selection process can favor approaches tailored to the repeatedly observed holdout. prompt: An equity team predicts next-month returns from company financial statements. The PM proposes using raw revenue alone, while an analyst argues that revenue growth and profit margin may better compare firms of different sizes. The team must improve the signal without incorporating information unavailable on the prediction date.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Revenue growth can capture a change over time that a single revenue level does not express directly.
statements.explanation: Growth represents a temporal relationship rather than only the current level.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Dividing profit by revenue may create a scale-adjusted feature that is more comparable across firms.
statements.explanation: A margin normalizes profit by firm activity and can support cross-firm comparisons.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Every derived feature necessarily adds new information that was absent from the raw inputs.
statements.explanation: A transformation may merely restate existing information and can be redundant.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The dates on which financial statements became publicly available matter when constructing these features.
statements.explanation: Using figures before their publication would make the historical feature unavailable in practice.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Feature engineering is useful only for linear models and cannot help distance-based learners.
statements.explanation: Appropriate transformations can also improve distance measures and neighborhood structure.

prompt: A futures desk models daily returns using price and volume data. The head trader believes the effect of unusual volume may depend on whether price is rising or falling, but the current linear model includes only the two raw variables separately. The research team considers adding an interaction between return sign and relative volume. The team asks you to identify the flawed claims. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An interaction feature can represent a relationship that depends on the joint values of two inputs.
statements.explanation: Interactions encode joint effects beyond independent additive contributions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In a purely additive linear model, separate price and volume terms automatically represent every possible interaction between them.
statements.explanation: Separate linear terms do not generally express a multiplicative or conditional effect.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A price-direction-by-volume feature could allow high volume to have different implications in rising and falling markets.
statements.explanation: The engineered feature can distinguish the two market contexts.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding the interaction guarantees better out-of-sample performance.
statements.explanation: The added flexibility may help, do nothing, or overfit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The interaction should be computed using only information known when the trade decision is made.
statements.explanation: A deployable feature must respect the decision-time information set.

prompt: A credit fund uses days-to-maturity, coupon, and yield to predict bond price changes. A junior researcher wants to add dozens of polynomial terms because "more transformations let the model discover everything, " while the risk officer is concerned about instability and limited historical defaults. The team must balance representation against generalization.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A nonlinear transformation can make some curved relationships easier for a linear learner to represent.
statements.explanation: Transformed inputs can let a linear combination express nonlinear patterns.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding many polynomial features can increase model complexity and overfitting risk.
statements.explanation: More terms provide more opportunities to fit noise, especially with limited data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a transformation is calculated only from existing features, it cannot affect a model's predictions.
statements.explanation: Reexpressing inputs can materially change what a learner can fit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The usefulness of engineered terms should be assessed on data not used to fit or select them.
statements.explanation: Held-out evaluation is needed to estimate whether the terms generalize.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A complicated feature is preferable to a simple feature whenever it lowers training error.
statements.explanation: Lower training error alone does not establish out-of-sample value.

prompt: A multi-factor equity model utilizes a rolling 12-month Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Linear Regression to estimate the beta (β) of individual technology stocks relative to the Nasdaq 100 index. The model uses these rolling beta estimates as a primary feature to predict cross-sectional next-week returns. During a sudden, high-volatility market pivot, the model's predictive performance degrades rapidly, and an audit reveals that the estimated coefficients were highly unstable. For this question, mark each statement True if it is incorrect and False if it is accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The instability of the beta coefficients is a classic symptom of Non-Stationarity in financial time series, meaning the underlying statistical relationship between the individual stocks and the index is changing over time.
statements.explanation: Financial regimes are dynamic. A beta calculated during a low-volatility bull market will completely misrepresent an asset's systemic risk when a market shock occurs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using a fixed, rolling 12-month window completely eliminates the risk of non-stationarity because it forces the OLS regression to constantly discard obsolete historical data, ensuring a stable parameter space.
statements.explanation: Rolling windows mitigate, but do not eliminate, non-stationarity. If a structural break occurs within the current window, the OLS parameters will be a polluted average of two completely different regimes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This pipeline suffers from a structural flaw because standard OLS regression assumes that the underlying data- generating process is Stationary (constant mean and variance), an assumption that routinely breaks down during market regime shifts.
statements.explanation: OLS regression assumes that the residuals are homoscedastic and independent. When regimes shift, the parameters shift, violating the core assumption that the underlying distribution is invariant.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The rapid degradation in model performance is due to a Structural Break, where the historical covariance matrix calculated over the stable 12-month period fails to capture the sudden, step-function change in market dynamics.
statements.explanation: A structural break fundamentally changes the parameters of the system. The historical 12-month data acts as an anchor, preventing the model from recognizing the new structural reality until the old data drops out of the window.

statements.label: E
statements.text: To adapt this linear framework to a non-stationary environment without changing the feature definitions, the weights of the regression should be modified using an exponential decay factor that prioritizes recent observations over distant ones.
statements.explanation: Switching to an exponentially weighted moving regression or a state-space model (like a Kalman Filter) allows the parameter estimation to adapt dynamically to drifting distributions.

prompt: An algorithmic momentum portfolio uses a machine learning classifier to predict whether a stock index will experience a positive or negative return over the next 20 trading days. The raw feature input is the 50-day rolling variance of daily returns. The system evaluates this feature using an Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) Test, which rejects the null hypothesis of a unit root (p<0.01). Based on this result, the pipeline passes the raw rolling variance series directly into a deep neural network without further transformation. During a prolonged market regime shift, the model's accuracy collapses, and an internal audit reveals that the rolling variance feature exhibited severe structural drift. Which of the following statements correctly diagnoses why the ADF test failed to prevent this distribution shift, and identifies the correct mathematical remedy?

statements.label: A
statements.text: The ADF test is structurally incapable of detecting non-stationarity driven by stochastic trends, meaning it can only validate stationarity for series with fixed, deterministic linear trends.
statements.explanation: The ADF test is specifically designed to detect stochastic trends (unit roots). It handles deterministic trends by including a time-trend component (βt) in its test regression.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The rolling variance series failed to maintain stationarity because the ADF test requires a minimum window length of 252 trading days to properly evaluate the presence of a unit root in second-moment statistical features.
statements.explanation: There is no arbitrary 252-day structural minimum required by the ADF test framework; its validity depends on sample size, lag structure, and the underlying data-generating process, not a specific calendar constraint.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The rejection of the null hypothesis by the ADF test mathematically guarantees that all statistical moments—including the mean, variance, and unconditional autocovariance—are perfectly invariant over the entire backtest horizon.
statements.explanation: A rejected ADF test is not a blanket guarantee of absolute stationarity. It simply means the series does not exhibit a random walk; it can still suffer from structural breaks, heteroscedasticity, or seasonal non-stationarity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The collapse occurred because the ADF test assumes the underlying data follows a Gaussian distribution; when applied to bounded, non-negative features like rolling variance, the test produces a high rate of false negatives.
statements.explanation: While the standard Dickey-Fuller distribution assumes independent and identically distributed errors, the test does not mechanically fail or invert its error rates solely because a feature is bounded or non-negative.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The ADF test only checks for a specific type of non-stationarity (a unit root/stochastic trend in the mean); it can easily register a series as "stationary" even if the feature suffers from structural breaks or structural drift in its variance over time.
statements.explanation: This highlights a critical limitation of the test in feature engineering. A series can be mean-reverting (no unit root) but still have its underlying distribution warp due to regime shifts or variance changes, which the ADF test does not account for.

G2: Scaling and Normalization Effects

prompt: A wealth manager uses KNN to identify historical days similar to the current market. One input is daily return measured near 0.01, while another is trading volume measured in millions of shares. The PM asks why the neighbors appear to be determined almost entirely by volume.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Without scaling, a large-magnitude feature can dominate a Euclidean distance calculation.
statements.explanation: Numerical magnitude directly affects distance unless the inputs are adjusted.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Standardizing the features can cause both return and volume to contribute on more comparable numerical scales.
statements.explanation: Standardization reduces dominance caused solely by differing units or ranges.

statements.label: C
